title: The Lymphatic and Immune Systems
description: Week 12, matched to the instructor's Exam 4 study guide: the lymph nodes and vessels, the bone marrow, thymus, tonsils, and spleen, the white blood cells and what each does, antibodies, memory cells, and vaccines, inflammation and its markers, and supporting immune health, with a case study.

wound.intro: A nurse in an urgent care clinic is caring for a 68-year-old client with a painful, swollen lower leg.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

Day 1, 0900: Client scraped the left shin on a garden fence 4 days ago. The area is now red, warm, swollen, and painful, about 10 cm across, with yellow drainage. Reports chills last night. Takes an herbal supplement “for immunity” and drinks two energy drinks a day. Has never had a pneumococcal vaccine. Walks the dog every day. Strong pulses in both ankles.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching how the body handles the small amount of fluid that leaks out of the blood capillaries into the tissues each day. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Arterioles pull it back in at the start of the next heartbeat
The kidneys draw it out of the tissues and excrete it
Sweat glands carry it to the skin, where it evaporates
Lymphatic vessels collect it and return it to the veins
questions.rationale:
Fluid that leaks into the tissues is picked up by lymphatic capillaries, which begin as dead-end tubes in the tissues. As lymph, it's filtered through nodes and returned to the veins, keeping fluid in balance.

The kidneys are the tempting choice, since they control the body's fluid, but they work on the blood, not directly on the fluid in the tissues.

Takeaway: The lymphatic system returns leaked tissue fluid to the blood; when it can't, the tissue swells.

questions.stem: After a client eats a meal high in fat, the lymph coming from the small intestine looks milky. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: White blood cells gather in the intestinal lining to digest the extra fat
Lacteals in the intestinal lining absorb dietary fats into the lymph
The liver sends bile into the lymph to break the fat down
The spleen releases stored fat into the lymph after a meal
questions.rationale:
Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries in the lining of the small intestine. They absorb dietary fats, which make the lymph there milky (chyle), and carry them toward the bloodstream.

Bile is the tempting choice, since bile helps digest fat, but it's released into the intestine, not into the lymph.

Takeaway: Fat absorption is one of the lymphatic system's three jobs, through the lacteals.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how lymph moves. For each description, click to specify the structure it describes.
rows: Carries filtered lymph away from a lymph node
Drains lymph from the right arm and the right side of the head
Carries unfiltered lymph toward a lymph node
Drains lymph from both legs, the abdomen, and the left arm
questions.rationale:
Afferent vessels carry unfiltered lymph toward a node, and efferent vessels carry filtered lymph away. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper body: the right arm, right upper trunk, and right side of the head and neck. The thoracic duct drains everything else.

The tempting mistake is swapping afferent and efferent. Think of afferent as arriving at the node and efferent as exiting it.

Takeaway: Afferent arrives, efferent exits. The right duct drains the right upper body; the thoracic duct drains the rest.

questions.stem: Place the path of fluid that leaves a capillary in the foot and returns to the blood in order.
items: Interstitial fluid around the cells of the foot
A vein at the base of the neck
questions.rationale:
Tissue fluid enters a lymphatic capillary, travels in an afferent vessel to a lymph node for filtering, leaves in an efferent vessel, and joins the thoracic duct, which empties into a vein at the base of the neck.

The tempting mistake is placing the duct before the node; the lymph is filtered in nodes along the way before it reaches the large ducts.

Takeaway: Tissue fluid, lymphatic capillary, afferent vessel, node, efferent vessel, duct, vein.

questions.stem: A client with strep throat has tender, swollen lymph nodes. Click a group of lymph nodes that would most likely be swollen.
questions.alt: Front view of the neck and trunk, with the client's right on the viewer's left: clusters of green nodes on each side of the neck, in each armpit, and along each groin crease; a short green vessel at the base of the neck on the viewer's left; a long, wide green vessel rising from a small green sac in the upper abdomen to the base of the neck on the viewer's right; a blue gland in the upper chest above the heart; a purple-red organ under the diaphragm on the viewer's right; blue veins at the base of the neck; and the faint lungs and heart.
questions.rationale:
Lymph from the throat drains to the cervical nodes along the sides of the neck, which swell as their lymphocytes respond to the infection. Either side counts.

The axillary nodes are the tempting choice, since they're another familiar group, but they drain the arms and the chest wall, not the throat.

Takeaway: Nodes swell near the infection they drain: throat to cervical, arm to axillary, leg to inguinal.

questions.stem: A client has an infected cut on the left foot, with red streaks running up the leg. Click the lymph node group shown here that is most likely to swell.
questions.alt: Front view of the neck and trunk, with the client's right on the viewer's left: clusters of green nodes on each side of the neck, in each armpit, and along each groin crease; a short green vessel at the base of the neck on the viewer's left; a long, wide green vessel rising from a small green sac in the upper abdomen to the base of the neck on the viewer's right; a blue gland in the upper chest above the heart; a purple-red organ under the diaphragm on the viewer's right; blue veins at the base of the neck; and the faint lungs and heart.
questions.rationale:
Lymph from the foot and leg drains to the inguinal nodes in the groin, on the same side: the left, which is on the viewer's right in a front view. Red streaks show lymphangitis, inflammation of the lymph vessels carrying the infection toward those nodes.

The inguinal group on the viewer's left is the tempting choice for students who forget to flip the sides: that's the client's right.

Takeaway: Leg infections drain to the inguinal nodes on the same side; in a front view, the client's left is on your right.

questions.stem: Click the vessel that returns most of the body's lymph to the blood.
questions.alt: Front view of the neck and trunk, with the client's right on the viewer's left: clusters of green nodes on each side of the neck, in each armpit, and along each groin crease; a short green vessel at the base of the neck on the viewer's left; a long, wide green vessel rising from a small green sac in the upper abdomen to the base of the neck on the viewer's right; a blue gland in the upper chest above the heart; a purple-red organ under the diaphragm on the viewer's right; blue veins at the base of the neck; and the faint lungs and heart.
questions.rationale:
The thoracic duct, the large vessel rising from the cisterna chyli in the abdomen, carries lymph from the legs, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head and chest, and empties into a vein at the base of the neck on the client's left.

The short right lymphatic duct is the tempting choice, since it's also a duct, but it drains only the right upper part of the body.

Takeaway: The thoracic duct drains most of the body; the right lymphatic duct drains the right upper part.

questions.stem: A tumor is blocking a client's thoracic duct. Which area should the nurse expect to still drain normally?
options: The left arm and the left side of the head, neck, and chest
Both legs and the lower abdomen
The right arm and the right side of the head and neck
The small intestine, including the lacteals
questions.rationale:
The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm, the right upper trunk, and the right side of the head and neck, so lymph from there doesn't pass through the thoracic duct and still drains.

The left arm and left side of the head are the tempting choice, since they're also the upper body, but they drain through the thoracic duct, as do the legs, abdomen, and intestines.

Takeaway: Only the right upper body bypasses the thoracic duct, through the right lymphatic duct.

questions.stem: Click the largest organ of the lymphatic system.
questions.alt: Front view of the neck and trunk, with the client's right on the viewer's left: clusters of green nodes on each side of the neck, in each armpit, and along each groin crease; a short green vessel at the base of the neck on the viewer's left; a long, wide green vessel rising from a small green sac in the upper abdomen to the base of the neck on the viewer's right; a blue gland in the upper chest above the heart; a purple-red organ under the diaphragm on the viewer's right; blue veins at the base of the neck; and the faint lungs and heart.
questions.rationale:
The spleen, the largest lymphatic organ, lies in the upper left abdomen (the left hypochondriac region), between the stomach and the diaphragm, on the viewer's right in a front view.

The thymus is the tempting choice, since it's also a lymphoid organ, but it's a small gland in the upper chest.

Takeaway: The spleen: the largest lymphatic organ, in the left upper abdomen under the diaphragm.

questions.stem: After a car crash, a client has fractures of the left 9th to 11th ribs, pain in the left upper abdomen, a heart rate of 124/min, and a blood pressure of 88/52 mm Hg. Which organ should the nurse suspect is bleeding?
options: The liver
The appendix
The gallbladder
The spleen
questions.rationale:
The spleen sits in the left upper abdomen, behind the left 9th to 11th ribs. It's spongy and full of blood, so an injury can bleed heavily, causing a fast heart rate and a falling blood pressure.

The liver is the tempting choice, since it also bleeds heavily when injured, but it sits on the right side, under the right ribs.

Takeaway: Left lower rib fractures with signs of bleeding: think of the spleen.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the spleen. For each function, click to specify the part of the spleen that carries it out.
rows: Filters old and damaged red blood cells out of the blood
Produces and matures lymphocytes
Stores platelets and white blood cells for release when needed
Processes antigens to start an immune response
questions.rationale:
White pulp is the spleen's immune tissue: it produces and matures lymphocytes and processes antigens. Red pulp filters the blood, removing old red cells, and holds a reserve of white cells and platelets.

The tempting mistake is linking stored white blood cells with the white pulp, since the names match, but the reserve is held in the red pulp.

Takeaway: White pulp: immune work. Red pulp: filtering and storage.

questions.stem: In the thymus, developing T cells that react strongly against the body's own tissues are destroyed. What does this process protect against?
options: Autoimmune disease
Allergic reactions to pollen
Viral infections
Lymphedema
questions.rationale:
This is negative selection: the thymus screens out T cells that would attack the body's own tissues, protecting against autoimmune disease.

Allergic reactions are the tempting choice, since they're also unwanted immune responses, but they're overreactions to outside substances, like pollen, not attacks on the body's own cells.

Takeaway: The thymus removes self-attacking T cells, guarding against autoimmunity.

questions.stem: A child has frequent sore throats, and the provider mentions the tonsils. Which explanation of the tonsils' role should the nurse give?
options: They make the saliva that begins digesting food
They close the airway when the child swallows
They're lymphoid tissue that traps germs from the mouth and nose
They warm and moisten the air before it moves down into the lungs
questions.rationale:
The tonsils are lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat. They trap pathogens entering through the mouth and nose and start immune responses.

Closing the airway is the tempting choice, since the tonsils sit near the throat, but that's the epiglottis's job.

Takeaway: Tonsils guard the entrance of the throat as lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how T cells mature in the thymus. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: In the thymus, {{0}} keeps the T cells that can recognize the body's own markers, and {{1}} destroys the T cells that would attack the body's own tissues.

options: clonal expansion
positive selection
phagocytosis
negative selection
opsonization
antigen presentation

questions.rationale:
Positive selection keeps T cells that can recognize the body's own markers, and negative selection removes those that react against the body's own tissues. Most developing T cells don't pass, and only those that pass both leave the thymus.

Clonal expansion is the tempting choice for the first blank, since it also increases useful T cells, but it happens later, when mature T cells meet a pathogen.

Takeaway: Positive selection keeps useful T cells; negative selection removes self-attacking ones.

questions.stem: A client asks why an inflamed ankle is swollen. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The injured muscle swells up as it gets stronger during healing.”
“Blood vessels in the ankle tighten up, which traps extra blood and fluid in the area.”
“The ankle's lymph nodes fill with fluid to fight the injury.”
“Chemicals like histamine make the small vessels leaky, so fluid moves into the tissue.”
questions.rationale:
Inflammatory mediators, like histamine and kinins, increase the permeability of the small vessels, so fluid and proteins leak into the tissue, causing swelling. Widened vessels also bring redness and warmth.

Vessels tightening is the tempting choice, since it sounds like a way to trap fluid, but inflammation widens the vessels; that's what makes the area red and warm.

Takeaway: Inflammation: wider vessels bring redness and heat; leaky vessels bring swelling.

questions.stem: Place the steps by which white blood cells leave the blood to reach an infection in order.
items: Chemical signals attract white blood cells to the area
The cells roll along the inner wall of the vessel
The cells stick tightly to the vessel wall
The cells squeeze through the vessel wall into the tissue
questions.rationale:
Leukocyte extravasation goes: chemoattraction, rolling adhesion, tight adhesion, and transmigration through the vessel wall into the tissue.

The tempting mistake is putting the tight adhesion first; cells have to slow down by rolling before they can stick firmly.

Takeaway: Attract, roll, stick, squeeze through.

questions.stem: A client develops itchy, raised welts (hives) after eating shellfish. Which cells should the nurse recognize as the source of the histamine causing the itching and swelling?
options: Red blood cells in the circulation
Mast cells in the skin and tissues
Platelets at the site of the welts
Neutrophils arriving from the blood
questions.rationale:
Mast cells are resident cells in the tissues that act as sentinels. When triggered, they release histamine, which makes vessels leaky and causes itching and swelling, as in hives.

Neutrophils are the tempting choice, since they're the most common white cells, but they fight acute bacterial infection by phagocytosis; histamine comes from mast cells and basophils.

Takeaway: Histamine comes from mast cells and basophils: itching, leaky vessels, and swelling.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client's wound for signs of acute inflammation. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Redness
Coolness of the skin
Swelling
Numbness
Pain
Warmth
questions.rationale:
The signs of acute inflammation are redness and warmth (from widened vessels), swelling (from leaky vessels), pain (from mediators like kinins), and loss of function.

Numbness is the tempting choice, since swelling can press on nerves, but inflammation typically causes pain, not numbness. Coolness is the opposite of what widened vessels bring.

Takeaway: Inflammation: redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lymphocytes. For each function, click to specify the lymphocyte that carries it out.
rows: Makes antibodies after it becomes a plasma cell
Directly kills virus-infected and cancer cells
Keeps immune cells from attacking the body's own cells
Activates B cells and killer T cells
questions.rationale:
B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies (humoral immunity). Killer (CD8+) T cells directly kill infected and cancer cells. Helper (CD4+) T cells activate B cells and killer T cells. Regulatory T cells keep the immune system from attacking the body.

The tempting mistake is giving antibody production to the helper T cells, since they're needed for it, but they activate the B cells, which make the antibodies.

Takeaway: B cells make antibodies; CD8+ T cells kill; CD4+ T cells help; regulatory T cells restrain.

questions.stem: Which cells in the lungs engulf inhaled dust and microbes?
options: Alveolar macrophages
Kupffer cells
Microglia
Plasma cells
questions.rationale:
Macrophages, which develop from monocytes, have different names in different tissues: alveolar macrophages in the lungs, Kupffer cells in the liver, and microglia in the nervous system.

Kupffer cells are the tempting choice, since they're also macrophages, but they live in the liver.

Takeaway: Macrophages by location: alveolar (lungs), Kupffer (liver), microglia (nervous system).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing dendritic cells. Which description of their role should the nurse give?
options: They make antibodies that circulate in the blood and lymph
They release heparin to keep the blood from clotting at an infection site
They form scar tissue after an infection heals
They capture antigens in the tissues and carry them to the lymph nodes
questions.rationale:
Dendritic cells live in tissues that meet the outside world, like the skin, nose, lungs, and intestines. They capture antigens, migrate to the lymph nodes, and present them to T cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

Making antibodies is the tempting choice, since dendritic cells start the specific response, but antibodies come from B cells (plasma cells).

Takeaway: Dendritic cells are messengers: they carry antigens from the tissues to T cells in the nodes.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a very low neutrophil count. Which risk should the nurse focus on?
options: Bleeding, since neutrophils help blood clot
Allergic reactions, since neutrophils control the release of histamine
Anemia, since neutrophils carry oxygen
Infection, since neutrophils are the first defense against bacteria
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils, 50% to 70% of white cells, are the first to reach an infection and destroy bacteria by phagocytosis. Too few means a high risk of infection.

Bleeding is the tempting choice, since chemotherapy can lower platelets too, but platelets, not neutrophils, help blood clot.

Takeaway: Low neutrophils mean high infection risk; low platelets mean bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A client vaccinated against measles is exposed to the virus but doesn't get sick. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: The vaccine's antibodies stay in the blood for life
The vaccine made the client's innate defenses stronger and faster
Memory cells from the vaccine respond quickly to the virus
The virus can't enter the cells of a vaccinated person
questions.rationale:
A vaccine trains the adaptive immune system, which keeps memory B and T cells. On exposure, they recognize the virus and respond quickly and strongly, before it can cause illness.

Antibodies staying for life is the tempting choice, but antibodies fade over time; protection lasts because memory cells can quickly make more.

Takeaway: Vaccines work through memory: a faster, stronger response the next time.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the classes of antibodies (immunoglobulins). For each description, click to specify the antibody.
rows: Found in tears, saliva, and breast milk
The first antibody made after a new exposure
The most common antibody in the blood
Defends against parasites and triggers allergic reactions
questions.rationale:
IgA protects body secretions, like tears, saliva, and colostrum. IgM is the first antibody made in a new response. IgG is the most common antibody in the blood, about 75%. IgE defends against parasites and drives allergic reactions.

The tempting mistake is calling IgG the first antibody, since it's the most common, but IgM comes first and IgG follows.

Takeaway: IgA in secretions, IgM first, IgG most common, IgE for parasites and allergy.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks the difference between an antigen and an antibody. Which response is accurate?
options: “An antigen is a protein made by B cells, and an antibody is a marker found on a germ.”
“An antigen is a marker on a germ or cell; an antibody is a protein that binds it.”
“Antigens and antibodies are two names for the same protective protein.”
“An antigen is a type of white blood cell; an antibody is what it releases.”
questions.rationale:
An antigen is a marker, found on viruses, bacteria, tumors, and the body's own cells, that the immune system recognizes. An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a protective protein that binds to a specific antigen.

Reversing the two is the tempting choice, since the words sound alike; remember that the antibody acts against the antigen.

Takeaway: Antigen: the marker. Antibody: the protein that binds it.

questions.stem: A client asks, “Why did I get so sick from a new virus before my body fought it off?” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Your body had no defenses against it until you took a medicine for it.”
“The virus shut down your immune system for the whole first week of the illness.”
“Your body's specific defenses take 4 to 7 days to build up against a new germ.”
“Your body starts fighting a virus after you've had a fever for several days.”
questions.rationale:
The innate immune system responds right away, but the adaptive system, which targets a specific germ, takes about 4 to 7 days to mount a strong response the first time. After that, memory cells make later responses faster.

No defenses until the medicine is the tempting choice, since the client felt so sick, but innate defenses were working from the start; the specific response just takes days.

Takeaway: First exposure: innate right away, adaptive in about 4 to 7 days. Later exposures: memory makes it fast.

questions.stem: A client with severe influenza develops a high fever, widespread inflammation, and failing organs. The provider describes a cytokine storm. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: The immune system releases cytokines out of control, harming its own tissues
The virus releases toxins that keep the client's cytokines from working normally
The client's immune system has stopped producing cytokines
The client's antibodies are attacking the influenza vaccine
questions.rationale:
A cytokine storm (hypercytokinemia) is an uncontrolled release of cytokines by the immune system. The inflammation it causes can damage organs; it has been seen in severe influenza, COVID-19, and acute pancreatitis.

Stopped producing cytokines is the tempting choice, since the client is so sick, but the problem is too much of the immune response, not too little.

Takeaway: A cytokine storm is the immune system overreacting, harming the body it's protecting.

questions.stem: A client with HIV asks why the infection makes it hard to fight off other germs. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “HIV infects and destroys helper T cells, which direct the rest of the immune system.”
“HIV destroys your red blood cells, so less oxygen reaches the immune cells.”
“HIV blocks your skin from acting as a barrier against germs.”
“HIV makes your body produce too many antibodies, which slowly wear out the immune system.”
questions.rationale:
HIV invades helper (CD4+) T cells. As their number falls, B cells and killer T cells aren't activated well, and cell-mediated immunity weakens, so other infections take hold.

Too many antibodies is the tempting choice, since the immune system is clearly involved, but the problem is the loss of helper T cells that coordinate the response.

Takeaway: HIV destroys CD4+ helper T cells, which weakens the whole adaptive response.

questions.stem: Leukemia cells have filled a client's bone marrow, crowding out the normal cells. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Fatigue from fewer red cells, with normal white cells
Clots in the legs from too many platelets
Frequent infections, easy bruising, and fatigue
Swollen neck nodes, with normal blood counts
questions.rationale:
The bone marrow makes all the blood cells: red cells, white cells, and platelets. When it's crowded out, all three fall: fewer white cells (infections), fewer platelets (bruising and bleeding), and fewer red cells (fatigue).

Fatigue with normal white cells is the tempting choice, since anemia is the best-known effect, but the marrow makes every blood cell line, so all of them drop.

Takeaway: Bone marrow failure lowers red cells, white cells, and platelets together.

questions.stem: A client scheduled for a bone marrow biopsy asks what the marrow does. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “It makes all your blood cells, and it's where B cells mature.”
“It filters your blood and removes your old red cells.”
“It's where your T cells mature and learn to spare your body.”
“It filters lymph and traps germs before they reach the blood.”
questions.rationale:
All blood cells form from stem cells in the bone marrow, and B cells also mature there.

Where T cells mature is the tempting choice, since T cells do form in the marrow, but they mature in the thymus. Filtering the blood is the spleen's job, and filtering lymph is the lymph nodes'.

Takeaway: Bone marrow: all blood cells form there; B cells mature there; T cells mature in the thymus.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing where white blood cells mature. For each cell, click to specify where it finishes maturing.
rows: Mast cell
Neutrophil
T cell
Macrophage (from a monocyte)
B cell
questions.rationale:
Every white cell starts in the bone marrow. Neutrophils and B cells finish maturing there; T cells finish in the thymus; mast cell precursors and monocytes leave the blood and mature in the tissues (monocytes become macrophages).

The tempting mistake is putting T cells in the bone marrow, since that's where they're made. Their training happens in the thymus.

Takeaway: Marrow: neutrophils, B cells. Thymus: T cells. Tissues: mast cells, macrophages.

questions.stem: A client with allergic asthma has a high eosinophil count. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Eosinophils join in allergy and asthma reactions, so they rise
Eosinophils fight bacteria, so the asthma must be from an infection
Eosinophils make antibodies, so the body is building immunity
Eosinophils carry oxygen, so they rise when breathing is hard
questions.rationale:
Eosinophils fight parasites and take part in allergic reactions and asthma, so a high count fits allergic asthma.

Fighting bacteria is the tempting choice, since a high white count often means infection, but bacteria raise neutrophils.

Takeaway: Eosinophils: parasites, allergies, asthma.

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing basophils and mast cells, since both release histamine. Which statement about them is accurate?
options: Basophils stay in the tissues; mast cells circulate in the blood
Both are lymphocytes that make antibodies against allergens
Both mature in the thymus before they enter the bloodstream
Basophils circulate in the blood; mast cells stay in the tissues
questions.rationale:
Basophils travel in the blood; mast cells live in the tissues (skin, airways, gut) as sentinels. Both release histamine, which makes vessels leaky and causes itching and swelling.

The reversed pair is the tempting choice, since the two cells are so alike. Remember that mast cells sit in place, guarding the tissues.

Takeaway: Basophils in the blood, mast cells in the tissues: both release histamine.

questions.stem: A client has had a long-lasting infection, and the monocyte count is high. Which role should the nurse expect these monocytes to play once they reach the infected tissue?
options: They become plasma cells that release antibodies
They become macrophages that engulf germs and dead cells
They release histamine that makes the nearby vessels leaky
They kill virus-infected cells without engulfing them
questions.rationale:
Monocytes leave the blood and become macrophages (or dendritic cells) in the tissues. Macrophages engulf germs, dead cells, and debris, and show antigens to T cells.

Plasma cells are the tempting choice, since they also develop from cells in the blood, but plasma cells come from B cells.

Takeaway: Monocytes become macrophages: the big eaters of the tissues.

questions.stem: A client's infected wound is draining thick, yellow pus. Which explanation of what pus is made of should the nurse give?
options: Dead red blood cells mixed with plasma
Antibodies that have bound tightly to the bacteria
Extra lymph that leaked from nearby nodes
Dead neutrophils, bacteria, and damaged tissue
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils are the first white cells to arrive and engulf bacteria; they die quickly, and their remains, with the bacteria and damaged tissue, form pus.

Antibodies is the tempting choice, since they bind bacteria too, but they're proteins dissolved in fluid, not the thick material of pus.

Takeaway: Pus is mostly dead neutrophils: a sign they've been fighting bacteria.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the stages of inflammation. For each description, click to specify the stage.
rows: Lasts about 2 to 6 weeks as healing continues
Is often quiet, but is linked to heart disease and diabetes
Starts within minutes of a cut, with redness, warmth, and swelling
Neutrophils are the first white cells to arrive
Goes on for months, with macrophages and lymphocytes causing slow damage
questions.rationale:
Acute inflammation starts within minutes to hours and lasts days: redness, warmth, swelling, and pain, with neutrophils arriving first, then macrophages. Subacute inflammation lasts about 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic inflammation lasts months or longer; macrophages and lymphocytes keep it going, and it's linked to heart disease, diabetes, and arthritis.

The tempting mistake is calling chronic inflammation the red, swollen kind. Chronic inflammation is usually low-grade and quiet.

Takeaway: Acute: fast and red, neutrophils. Subacute: 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic: quiet and long, macrophages and lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the cytokines of inflammation. For each action, click to specify the cytokine group that performs it.
rows: Released by virus-infected cells to warn the cells nearby
Form a trail that draws neutrophils to an infection
Made mostly by macrophages; very large amounts can cause shock
Carry messages between white cells; some cause fever
questions.rationale:
Interferons come from virus-infected cells and help nearby cells resist the virus. Chemokines call white cells to a site. Tumor necrosis factor, mostly from macrophages, drives inflammation and fever, and too much at once can cause shock. Interleukins pass messages between white cells; IL-1 and IL-6 cause fever.

The tempting mix-up is between chemokines and interleukins, since both are messages. Chemokines specifically make cells move toward the site.

Takeaway: Chemokines call, interferons fight viruses, interleukins message, TNF inflames.

questions.stem: A client asks how the immune system can recognize a new virus it has never met before. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Your immune cells copy the virus's shape after it infects you, and then attack it.”
“Each of your B and T cells has its own receptor, so some match almost any germ.”
“The antibodies from your past infections attach to any new virus that enters.”
“Your body spots a new virus by its size, since viruses look alike.”
questions.rationale:
This is the result of heterogeneity: as lymphocytes develop, their receptor genes are shuffled and mutated, so each B and T cell carries a unique receptor. With so much variety, some cells match almost any germ, and those cells multiply when it appears.

Copying the virus's shape is the tempting choice, since the response is so specific, but the matching receptors already exist before the virus arrives; the virus selects them.

Takeaway: Receptor variety (heterogeneity) lets the immune system recognize germs it has never seen.

questions.stem: Two coworkers get the same vaccine. One makes high antibody levels, and the other makes much lower levels. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: People's immune responses vary with their genes, age, and health
The coworker with low levels must have had the infection already
The coworker with low levels is likely allergic to the vaccine
Antibody levels depend on which arm the vaccine was given in
questions.rationale:
The immune response is heterogeneous: people differ in their receptor genes, age, and health (for example, older adults and people on immune-suppressing drugs often respond less strongly), so the same vaccine can give different antibody levels.

A past infection is the tempting choice, but that would usually make the response stronger, since memory cells are already there.

Takeaway: People respond differently to the same germ or vaccine: one result of heterogeneity.

questions.stem: Two days after starting antibiotics for an infection, a client's C-reactive protein (CRP) has fallen by half, but the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is still high. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: The infection is getting worse, since the ESR is still high
The inflammation is easing; the ESR falls more slowly than CRP
The CRP result must be wrong, since both should fall together
A new infection has started, since the two results disagree
questions.rationale:
CRP rises within hours and falls quickly once inflammation settles. The ESR rises and falls more slowly, so it often lags behind. A falling CRP with a still-high ESR fits inflammation that's improving.

The infection is getting worse is the tempting choice, since the ESR is still high, but the faster-moving CRP is the better sign of the current trend.

Takeaway: CRP changes fast; ESR changes slowly. Follow the trend.

questions.stem: A client has a fever and a cough, and the provider orders a procalcitonin level. Which explanation of the test should the nurse give?
options: “It measures how fast your red cells settle in a tube, which shows inflammation.”
“It's a stress hormone level that shows how your body is coping.”
“It rises mostly with bacterial infections, which helps guide antibiotics.”
“It shows whether your prostate is inflamed or enlarged.”
questions.rationale:
Procalcitonin stays very low in health and rises sharply in bacterial infections and sepsis, while staying low in most viral infections. It helps the provider decide whether antibiotics are likely to help.

How fast red cells settle is the tempting choice, since it's another inflammation test, but that's the ESR, which doesn't tell bacteria from other causes.

Takeaway: Procalcitonin points toward bacterial infection; CRP and ESR show inflammation of any cause.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with a fever, pain on urination, and a tender prostate has a high prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level. The client asks whether this means cancer. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Yes; a high PSA level confirms that you have prostate cancer.”
“No; PSA rises with age and isn't linked to the prostate.”
“PSA rises with infections anywhere in the body, so it says little about the prostate.”
“An inflamed prostate can raise PSA too; the provider will follow up.”
questions.rationale:
PSA is made by normal and cancerous prostate cells. Cancer can raise it, but so can prostatitis (inflammation) and an enlarged prostate (BPH). With signs of prostatitis, the high PSA needs follow-up, not a conclusion.

“A high PSA confirms cancer” is the tempting choice, since PSA is used to screen for prostate cancer, but it isn't specific to cancer.

Takeaway: PSA rises with prostate cancer, BPH, and prostatitis.

questions.stem: A healthy 68-year-old client had all childhood vaccines. Which vaccines should the nurse recommend now?
options: No more vaccines, since childhood vaccines protect for a lifetime
Pneumococcal, shingles, and yearly flu and COVID-19 vaccines
A shingles vaccine alone, since it also protects against pneumonia
A tetanus booster alone, since the others are for children
questions.rationale:
The instructor's list: keep up with vaccines and a record of them: childhood vaccines, yearly flu and COVID-19 vaccines, and pneumococcal and shingles vaccines for older adults.

No more vaccines is the tempting choice, since the client is healthy, but protection from some childhood vaccines fades, and older adults face new risks like shingles and pneumonia.

Takeaway: Older adults: pneumococcal and shingles, plus yearly flu and COVID-19.

questions.stem: A college student drinks three energy drinks a day to stay awake for studying. Which explanation of how this affects health should the nurse give?
options: “Their caffeine strengthens your white cells against infection.”
“They supply the vitamins your immune cells need, so diet matters less.”
“Their sugar and artificial ingredients can promote inflammation.”
“They affect your sleep, but they have no effect on inflammation.”
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide names energy drinks as a lifestyle choice that harms health: they're high in sugar and artificial ingredients, which can lead to inflammation.

Supplying vitamins is the tempting choice, since some drinks add vitamins, but they don't replace whole foods, and the sugar works against the immune system.

Takeaway: Energy drinks: sugar and additives that promote inflammation.

questions.stem: A client says, “I take an herbal supplement for my immune system, so I don't need a flu shot.” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Use supplements only with your provider's guidance, and keep getting vaccines.”
“That's fine; herbal supplements protect you just as well as the flu shot does.”
“Herbal supplements are natural, so you can take as much as you like.”
“Stop the supplement, since herbs weaken the immune system.”
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide: herbal supplements can support immune health with the provider's guidance, as part of other healthy choices (exercise, a healthy diet, and vaccinations), never in place of them. Some interact with medications.

“Stop the supplement” is the tempting choice, since it sounds cautious, but the nurse's role is to involve the provider, not to forbid it; the key teaching is that it doesn't replace the vaccine.

Takeaway: Supplements: with the provider's guidance, alongside vaccines, diet, and exercise.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' notes that need follow-up.
questions.passage: Client [[scraped the left shin on a garden fence 4 days ago]]. The area is now [[red, warm, swollen, and painful]], [[about 10 cm across]], with [[yellow drainage]]. [[Reports chills last night]]. [[Takes an herbal supplement “for immunity”]] and [[drinks two energy drinks a day]]. [[Has never had a pneumococcal vaccine]]. [[Walks the dog every day]]. [[Strong pulses in both ankles]].
questions.rationale:
The red, warm, swollen, painful area with drainage and chills shows acute inflammation from an infection that's spreading into the body; its size is a baseline to track. The supplement needs the provider's review, the energy drinks feed inflammation, and the missing pneumococcal vaccine is a prevention gap.

The scrape on the fence is the tempting one to highlight, since it started everything, but it's the history, not something to act on now. Daily walks and strong pulses are reassuring.

Takeaway: Act on the signs of inflammation and infection, then the gaps in immune health.

questions.stem: For each laboratory result, click to specify what it most likely shows.
rows: White blood cells 15,800/mm³, with 82% neutrophils
C-reactive protein 9.6 mg/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/hr
Procalcitonin 1.8 ng/mL
Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL
questions.rationale:
A high white count driven by neutrophils, and a high procalcitonin, point to a bacterial infection. CRP and ESR show that inflammation is present but not its cause. The hemoglobin is normal.

The tempting mistake is reading a high CRP as proof of bacteria. CRP rises with any inflammation; procalcitonin is the more specific clue.

Takeaway: Neutrophils and procalcitonin: bacteria. CRP and ESR: inflammation of any cause.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The red, warm, swollen leg shows {{0}} inflammation. The white cells that arrive first are {{1}}, drawn to the site by {{2}}.

options: chronic
acute
subacute
macrophages
lymphocytes
neutrophils
chemokines
interferons
antibodies

questions.rationale:
Redness, warmth, swelling, and pain within days of an injury are acute inflammation. Neutrophils arrive first, followed by macrophages, following the trail of chemokines to the site.

Macrophages is the tempting choice, since they're key to inflammation, but they arrive after the neutrophils and clean up.

Takeaway: Acute inflammation: neutrophils first, called in by chemokines.

questions.stem: Before the client leaves, which teaching about immune health should the nurse include?
options: Ask the provider before continuing the herbal supplement
Replace the energy drinks with water
Ask about getting the pneumococcal vaccine
Eat mostly whole foods, like vegetables, fruits, and whole grains
Stop walking the dog for the next month
Double the herbal supplement while the infection lasts
questions.rationale:
The instructor's interventions: supplements with the provider's guidance, vaccinations (pneumococcal for older adults), a whole-food diet, and regular exercise; energy drinks promote inflammation.

Stopping the walks is the tempting choice, since the leg is sore, but regular exercise supports immune health; the client can rest the leg as the provider directs without giving up activity for a month.

Takeaway: Teach vaccines, whole foods, exercise, and supplements only with the provider's guidance.

questions.stem: Three days after starting antibiotics, the client returns. For each finding, click to specify whether it has improved, not changed, or gotten worse.
rows: Temperature: 38.6 °C then, 37.0 °C now
C-reactive protein: 9.6 mg/dL then, 3.1 mg/dL now
Procalcitonin: 1.8 ng/mL then, 0.4 ng/mL now
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 48 mm/hr then, 47 mm/hr now
Red area: 10 cm across then, 14 cm across now
questions.rationale:
The fever, CRP, and procalcitonin are all falling, which fits an infection responding to treatment. The ESR hasn't changed, which is expected, since it falls slowly. But the red area has grown, so the infection may be spreading at the edges: report it.

The tempting mistake is calling everything improved because the labs are better. A spreading area of redness needs follow-up even when the numbers improve.

Takeaway: Read every finding: improving markers don't cancel a spreading infection.
